questions.q: What is the main architectural difference between a CPU and a GPU?
options: CPUs have more total transistors than GPUs
CPUs have a few complex cores for fast single-task execution; GPUs have thousands of simple cores for parallel throughput
GPUs run at a higher clock speed than CPUs
CPUs cannot perform floating-point arithmetic
questions.explain: CPUs use a handful of large, complex cores optimized for fast sequential execution (latency-oriented). GPUs use thousands of simple cores optimized for total parallel throughput.

questions.q: Why does matrix multiplication map well onto GPU hardware?
options: Because matrix multiplication requires branching logic
Because each output element can be computed independently of the others, which is data parallelism
Because matrices are always small enough to fit in CPU cache
Because GPUs can only perform addition, not multiplication
questions.explain: Every element of a matrix multiplication's output can be computed without needing any other element's result — that independence is data parallelism, which thousands of simple GPU cores exploit well.

options: Optimizing for the fastest possible completion of a single task
Optimizing for the total amount of work completed per second across many tasks, even if any one task is slower to start
Optimizing for the lowest possible power consumption
Optimizing exclusively for integer arithmetic
questions.explain: Throughput-oriented design (the GPU's approach) prioritizes total work done per second in aggregate, rather than minimizing the time for any single task.

questions.q: A single NVIDIA A100 GPU has roughly how many CUDA cores compared to a high-end server CPU's core count?
options: About the same number
Roughly half as many
Over 100 times as many
GPUs don't have cores at all
questions.explain: An A100 has 6,912 CUDA cores versus roughly 64 cores on a high-end server CPU — a difference of more than 100x, which is the main source of GPU throughput advantage.

questions.q: What kind of workload is a GPU poorly suited for?
options: Large matrix multiplications
Element-wise operations applied to millions of values
Inherently sequential work where each step depends on the previous step's result
Convolution operations over image data
questions.explain: Sequential workloads with step-by-step dependencies and heavy branching don't parallelize, so they don't benefit from a GPU's thousands of simple cores and may run faster on a CPU.
